subject: Career
title: Positioning: Owning a Category
description: A micro-lesson that makes Positioning: Owning a Category usable.

hook.text: 'The AI ethics expert' or 'the startup CFO for biotech' — narrow positioning makes you the go-to person.

buildup.text: Al Ries and Jack Trout's 'Positioning' showed: you win by owning a category in people's minds.

discovery.text: Being 'a marketer' is forgettable. Being 'the growth marketer for B2B SaaS' is referable.

twist.text: Narrow positioning feels scary — 'I'll miss opportunities!' But generalists are never the first call.

climax.text: Pick a lane, dominate it, then expand. Don't try to be everything from day one.

punchline.text: Specialists get called. Generalists get compared.

quiz.question: Why is narrow professional positioning more effective than being a generalist?
options: It makes you the go-to person in a specific category
It's easier to learn one thing

details.summary: Positioning means deliberately claiming a specific niche in your audience's mind. Just as brands own categories in marketing, professionals who own a clear positioning are top-of-mind when relevant opportunities arise.
details.whyItMatters: Being known for something specific makes you the default choice when that need emerges. Generalists compete on price; specialists compete on irreplaceability.
takeaways: Choose a positioning narrow enough that you can credibly dominate it
Consistency across platforms reinforces your category ownership
Resist the temptation to broaden positioning too early

faq.question: How narrow should your professional positioning be?
faq.answer: Narrow enough that few competitors claim the same space, but broad enough that sufficient opportunities exist. If you can name five other people known for exactly the same thing, it is too broad. If opportunities arise less than quarterly, it may be too narrow.

faq.question: Can you have strong positioning without limiting future career options?
faq.answer: Yes. Strong positioning makes you the default for one category but does not prevent you from expanding later. Most successful career pivots are easier from a position of known expertise than from a position of vague generalism.
